## HP17 מדריך ההורים

Route: `/he/parents/guide`  
Search title: מדריך ההורים | שיתוף פעולה וליווי | BNA  
Search description: כיצד ההורים תומכים בהכנה ללימוד, במטרות, בתקשורת מכבדת ובעמידה בהתחייבויות בקהילת הלימוד של BNA.

### שיתוף פעולה עם ההורים

ההורה, התלמיד והמחנך מביאים ידע שונה לאותה שיחה. ההורים מכירים את ההיסטוריה ואת חיי היומיום של הילד. המחנך רואה את השתתפותו בסביבת הלימוד. הבן צריך להיות שותף להבנת הקושי ולקבלת אחריות על תגובתו.

### חיזוק הציפיות המשותפות

עזרו לבנכם להבין את ההתחייבויות שסוכמו עם הקבוצה. שוחחו על האופן שבו אחריות, כבוד ומחלוקת ראויה מתבטאים במצבים ממשיים. עודדו אותו לתאר את חלקו שלו, במקום לדבר בשמו בכל פעם שעולה קושי.

### עזרו לו להגיע מוכן

סייעו בהגעה בזמן, בהבאת החומרים הדרושים ובסידורים המעשיים של הבוקר. ככל שעצמאותו מתפתחת, העבירו אליו חלקים מתאימים מההכנה ובדקו אם הוא מבצע אותם בעקביות.

### שיתוף בתצפיות מועילות

ספרו למחנך מה אתם רואים בבית: שינויים בעניין, קושי להתארגן, דאגה בנוגע לקשר עם אדם אחר או התחייבות שקשה לשמור עליה. תצפיות ממוקדות מקלות על ההסכמה על תמיכה מועילה.

### התמודדות משותפת עם קשיים

בררו את המצב לפני שמחליטים מה צריך לקרות בהמשך. תנו לבנכם זמן להסביר את נקודת מבטו. בחנו את התגובות האפשריות, את השפעתן הצפויה ואת ההתאמה שלהן לערכים ולהתחייבויות הנוגעים למצב.

הצעד הבא שסוכם צריך להיות ברור דיו כדי שאפשר יהיה לעקוב אחריו. בדקו מה קרה והתאימו את התמיכה לפי הצורך.

### למידה מטעויות

טעות יכולה להצביע על מיומנות שזקוקה לתרגול, על משימה שלא הובנה או על התחייבות שלא הייתה מציאותית. המטרה היא לעזור לבן להעריך את התוצאה ולנקוט את הצעד האחראי הבא.

המבוגרים שומרים על גבולות מתאימים, ובה בעת מאפשרים לתלמיד לחוות את תוצאותיהן של החלטות שהוא מסוגל להתמודד איתן. הליווי מפתח את שיקול דעתו לאורך זמן.

### בחירת מסגרת השיחה המתאימה

עניינים אישיים הנוגעים ללימוד, להתנהגות ולמשפחה נידונים בפרטיות עם המחנך. שיחות קהילתיות עוסקות בסידורים ובתחומי עניין משותפים. מידע פרטי על ילד אחר אינו שייך לקבוצת הורים או לאינדקס.

### בחינת ההתקדמות

שימו לב גם להישגים וגם לתנאים שבהם הושגו. משימה שהושלמה בעזרה, משימה שהושלמה באופן עצמאי ואחריות שנשמרה בעקביות הן צורות שונות של התקדמות.

השיחה בין ההורה למחנך צריכה להבהיר את ההבחנות האלה ולזהות צעד מעשי להמשך.

קישורים: [תפקיד ההורים](#ha06-תפקיד-ההורים-בתוכנית-לימוד-תורה-אלטרנטיבית) · [קשרים בין הורים](#hp07-קשרים-בין-הורים) · [שאלות נפוצות](#hp16-שאלות-נפוצות)

## HP18 מדריך ההשתתפות לתלמיד

Route: `/he/learning-pods/participation`  
Search title: השתתפות התלמידים | אקדמיית בני נביאים  
Search description: התחייבויות לימודיות, אוטונומיה, מחלוקת מכבדת, שמירה על מרחבים משותפים וליווי בקהילת BNA.

### אוטונומיה ואחריות משותפת

לרעיונות, לשאלות ולהחלטות שלך יש חשיבות. להיות חלק מקהילת הלימוד פירושו גם לקבל אחריות על ההתחייבויות שלך ולהתחשב בהשפעת המעשים שלך על אחרים.

### התחייבויות בלימוד

סכם עם המחנך על התחייבות שמתאימה לרמתך הנוכחית ומאפשרת צעד משמעותי להמשך. ודא שאתה מבין מה היא כוללת ואיזו עזרה זמינה.

אם מתעורר קושי, דבר עם המחנך. הסבר מה קרה כדי שאפשר יהיה לקבוע את הצעד הבא ולעקוב אחריו.

### שאלות ומחלוקת

שאל שאלות והסבר את דעתך. הקשב לתשובה המלאה ואפשר לאחרים לדבר. מחלוקת היא הזדמנות להבין טוב יותר מקור או את שיקול הדעת של אדם אחר.

עלבונות, הפחדה והפרעות מונעים מאחרים ללמוד, ויש לטפל בהם.

### המרחב והציוד המשותפים

השתמש בציוד כראוי, החזר את מה שלקחת והשלם את חלקך בהכנת המרחב או בהחזרתו למצב מסודר. עדכן את המחנך אם משהו חסר, ניזוק או דורש טיפול.

### תנועה והשתתפות

ברר את הגבולות המוסכמים ליציאה להפסקה או ממפגש לימוד. הישאר במסגרת שבה מתקיימת השגחה, ועדכן את המחנך כאשר אתה זקוק לעזרה. יציאה מהמקום דורשת את הסידורים שסוכמו עם המבוגרים האחראים.

### ליווי ובחינת ההתקדמות

בחן מה התכוונת לעשות, מה עשית בפועל ומה השפיע על התוצאה. ההתחייבות הבאה צריכה להתבסס על מה שאתה כבר מסוגל לעשות ולתת מענה לקושי שדורש תשומת לב.

קבלת אחריות כוללת הכרה בטעות, תיקון של מה שאפשר לתקן וניסיון של צעד מתאים להמשך.

### יצירת קשר עם BNA

ספרו על מה תרצו לשוחח וכיצד אפשר ליצור איתכם קשר. שלומי יחזור אליכם אישית.

### הודעת הפרטיות של אקדמיית בני נביאים

הודעה זו מסבירה מהו המידע המשמש לטיפול בפניות דרך אתר BNA, בהתעניינות בקבוצות הלימוד ובאקדמיה, בקשרים בין הורים, בפניות של נותני שירות, בבקשות טכנולוגיה, בפניות לתמיכה ובהמשך הטיפול הקשור אליהן.

### יצירת קשר

לשאלות על המידע שלכם, לתיקונים או לעדכון העדפות תקשורת, פנו לשלומי דרטלר בכתובת [office@bneineviimacademy.org](mailto:office@bneineviimacademy.org). אפשר לכתוב בשורת הנושא ״בקשת פרטיות״. אין צורך בחשבון מקוון כדי להגיש בקשה.

### המידע שאתם מוסרים

בהתאם לטופס, BNA מקבלת את שמכם, כתובת הדוא״ל או מספר הטלפון, אזור המגורים הכללי, השפה ואמצעי המענה המועדפים, ואת ההודעה ששלחתם. הורה או אפוטרופוס עשוי למסור גם את גיל הילד, תחומי העניין שלו בלימוד ותיאור קצר של התמיכה החינוכית המבוקשת.

בטפסים לנותני שירות ולמחנכים מתבקשים פרטים מקצועיים רלוונטיים. בבקשות טכנולוגיה מתבקשים פרטים על בית הספר או הארגון ועל תהליך העבודה שתרצו לבחון. בטפסי תמיכה נשאל כיצד תרצו לתרום.

הטפסים הציבוריים מיועדים למבוגרים. אין לצרף רשומות רפואיות, אבחנות מפורטות, היסטוריית תרופות, מספרי תעודות מזהות, סיסמאות, פרטי כרטיסי תשלום או מידע פרטי על ילד אחר. אם בשלב מאוחר יותר של התוכנית יידרש מידע רגיש, המטרה וההליך המתאים יוסברו בנפרד.

### תיעוד פניות ותקשורת

BNA שומרת את המידע הדרוש למענה על פנייה, לתיעוד שיחות רלוונטיות ולמעקב אחר צעד שסוכם. הרשומות עשויות לכלול את נושא הפנייה, מועד השליחה, מספר סימוכין, העדפות ואת ההודעה או בחירות ההרשאה הקשורות לשליחה.

האתר משתמש גם במידע טכני הדרוש להפעלת טפסים, לשמירה על רצף השימוש באתר, למניעת שליחות כפולות, לזיהוי שגיאות ולהגנה על השירות. מידע זה עשוי לכלול זמני בקשות, מידע על המכשיר או הדפדפן, כתובות IP ומזהי חיבור נחוצים. מידע על מקור ההפניה עשוי לזהות את העמוד או מסע הפרסום שדרכם הגיעה הפנייה.

### כיצד נעשה שימוש במידע

המידע משמש למענה לבקשה שלכם, לדיון בהתאמה ובסידורים, לתיאום המשך טיפול רלוונטי ולשמירה על רישום מנהלי מדויק. במידע הנחוץ נעשה שימוש גם לאבטחת השירות, לטיפול בשגיאות, למענה לבקשות פרטיות ולעמידה בחובות החלות על הפעילות.

הרשמה חינמית להתעניינות פותחת שיחה. היא אינה רושמת ילד לתוכנית, מאשרת תשלום, יוצרת חשבון תלמיד או רושמת את המשפחה אצל נותן שירות חיצוני.

### בחירות בנוגע לתקשורת

בקשה ליצירת קשר מאפשרת ל־BNA להשיב בנוגע לאותה בקשה. קבלת מאמרים חינוכיים, עדכונים קהילתיים או הודעות שיווקיות אחרות לבחירתכם דורשת בחירה נפרדת עבור המטרה והערוץ המתאימים.

אפשר לבקש להפסיק הודעות שאינן חובה או לעדכן פרטי קשר. שינוי העדפה אינו מונע תקשורת הנחוצה למענה על פנייה קיימת או לניהול הסדר שהצטרפתם אליו.

### קשרים בין הורים

פנייה פרטית אינה רישום באינדקס. פרטי קשר נמסרים לצורך היכרות בין הורים רק בהסכמה נפרדת על הפרטים ועל מי שיקבל אותם. אפשר לבקש מ־BNA לשנות או להסיר את הפרטים שהסכמתם לשתף.

רשומות משפחתיות פרטיות, תצפיות על תלמידים ומידע על הלימוד נפרדים מהיכרות בין הורים ומרישומים קהילתיים.

### נותני שירות ועסקים אחרים

נותני שירות עצמאיים אחראים לשירותים שלהם ולמידע שנאסף בתהליכי ההרשמה או יצירת הקשר שלהם. פנייה של נותן שירות ל־BNA נפרדת מההחלטה לפרסם את פרטיו העסקיים באינדקס.

ל־Fishing Academy יש הרשמה, תוכנית ויישומון נפרדים. מידע על התהליך שלה מופיע בהודעה המצורפת לטופס שלה. התעניינות ב־BNA אינה יוצרת אוטומטית פנייה ל־Fishing Academy.

### שירותים המשמשים להפעלת BNA

מידע רלוונטי עשוי להיות מטופל באמצעות שירותים המשמשים לאחסון האתר, לשמירת מידע, לתקשורת, לניהול או להליך תשלום מורשה. יש להגביל את הגישה למטרה שלשמה נעשה שימוש בשירות. ספקים עשויים לעבד מידע מחוץ למדינה או לארץ שבהן אתם מתגוררים.

מידע פרטי על תלמידים או משפחות אינו מתפרסם באינדקס נותני השירות. הוא אינו נמסר למשפחות אחרות רק משום שהן משתמשות באותו אתר או באותה פלטפורמה.

### בקשות טכנולוגיה ובינה מלאכותית

לפנייה הטכנולוגית הראשונה נדרש תיאור כללי בלבד של המשימה. אין לצרף רשומות תלמידים פרטיות, מידע סודי של בית הספר או פרטי גישה לחשבונות.

כל פרויקט בהמשך הכולל מידע כזה דורש הגדרת היקף עבודה, הסדרי גישה ובדיקה משלו. פנייה בנוגע לטכנולוגיה אינה מאשרת הקלטת שיעור, יצירת פרופילים של תלמידים או שימוש ברשומות פרטיות בתהליך עבודה של בינה מלאכותית.

### תמיכה ותשלומים

פנייה לתמיכה או התחייבות לתרומה מתועדת כפנייה או כהתחייבות, ולא כתרומה שהושלמה. אם נעשה שימוש בשירות תשלום מורשה, המידע הרלוונטי לעסקה עשוי לכלול פרטי קשר, סכום, מטבע, מצב התשלום ומספר סימוכין לעסקה. יש להזין פרטי כרטיס תשלום רק דרך שירות התשלום המזוהה, ולא בטופס פנייה כללי.

### שמירת מידע ובקשות

המידע נשמר בהתאם למטרת הרשומה, להסדרים מתמשכים ולדרישות מנהליות או משפטיות החלות עליו. בקשה לתיקון או להסרת מידע נבחנת בהקשר הזה. ייתכן שיהיה צורך לשמור רשומות מוגבלות כדי לתעד הסדר, ליישב מחלוקת או לכבד בקשה שלא לקבל הודעות שאינן חובה.

פנו ל־BNA כדי לשאול על המידע הקשור לפנייתכם, לבקש תיקון או לבטל בחירה לקבלת הודעות שאינן חובה או לשיתוף מידע. ייתכן שיידרש אימות נוסף כאשר הוא מתאים להגנה על המידע הנוגע לבקשה.

### עדכונים

ההודעה החלה על טופס צריכה להיות זמינה בעת מסירת המידע. אם מטרת השימוש במידע או אופן הטיפול בו משתנים באופן מהותי, יש לעדכן את ההודעה הרלוונטית ואת הבחירות הנדרשות לפני יישום השינוי.

Bnei Neviim uses personal goals, honest conversations, movement, and Torah discussion to help boys rebuild ownership. The adult does not disappear. The adult becomes a mentor who helps the boy think and choose.

A11.title: A Guide to Healthy Technology Use: Our Philosophy and Approach
A11.markdown:
## A11 A Guide to Healthy Technology Use: Our Philosophy and Approach

Route: `/blog/healthy-technology-use-jewish-children`  
Topic: Technology  
Search title: Healthy Technology Use for Jewish Children | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: A Torah-based approach to technology: abstinence, limited use, holistic use, and practical boundaries for children.

There are three basic philosophies to the approach of technology usage.

### The Abstinence Approach

The Abstinence Approach views technology as a significant distraction from spiritual growth. It advocates avoiding technology in order to focus on serving Hashem. This was my experience during my years in yeshiva, where I completely disconnected from technology, allowing me to fully immerse myself in Torah study.

**Pros:** The benefits of this approach can be profound, particularly for those who seek to excel in learning Gemara within a yeshiva setting. Engaging fully in Torah study without the distractions of technology allows time for concentration and spiritual connection. I found that commitment valuable in learning how to learn.

**Cons:** There are significant downsides to this approach. Professional life often involves tools such as messaging and email. Avoiding these tools can restrict the work a person is able to do and the educational material he can access. There is also a social question: how do we explain our boundaries to children without belittling people who live differently? A boundary that adults have chosen with conviction may be harder for their children to understand.

I personally know individuals who have chosen this path despite its challenges. They have made this decision with full awareness of the difficulties, guided by their Rabbis and driven by their commitment to what they believe is the best way to raise their children in a world where no ideology is foolproof. These individuals deserve great respect for the conviction behind their decision. I think of the verses שומר פתאים ה׳ and עדות ה׳ נאמנה מחכימת פתי, and the trust in Hashem expressed by that way of life.

### The Limited Use Approach

The Limited Use Approach advocates cautious engagement with technology, allowing its use for positive purposes while remaining vigilant against its dangers. In a conversation with Rabbi Daniel Travis, we discussed the distinction between broad warnings about internet use and a person's individual circumstances. During that conversation, he described internet use as a spiritual compromise that is often necessary for functioning in the modern world.

**Pros:** This approach provides access to online learning and tools for earning a livelihood. It was spectacular to witness during the COVID-19 pandemic when the lectures of renowned Rabbis reached students thousands of miles away through the internet.

**Cons:** The downside to this approach is that involvement with technology is experienced as a spiritual compromise. For some, this perspective helps maintain their commitment to spirituality without getting carried away. For others, it can leave a significant portion of their life feeling בדיעבד—less than ideal.

### The Holistic Approach

The Holistic Approach views technology as a powerful tool that Hashem created to enhance spiritual growth. This philosophy embraces technology as a means to access wisdom and disseminate positive messages. It incorporates the same safeguards as the previous approach but with a fundamental difference: the internet, technology, and physical engagement are seen as tools to be used for good, without inherently undermining a person's spiritual level. I connect this perspective with the emphasis in Chassidus on bringing avodas Hashem into physical life.

**Pros:** Wisdom that can aid in serving Hashem becomes something to seek out and put to use. Engaging with worthwhile material can be invigorating and can support a person's spiritual and practical goals.

**Cons:** Purposeful use still requires vigilance. A person can encounter inappropriate content or become involved in activities contrary to his values.

In practice, technology use should be tailored to an individual's stage of life and personal goals. If a person is in yeshiva and wants to immerse himself in learning, less technology may serve that goal. If someone needs the internet for work but struggles with its boundaries, the second approach may be appropriate.

Personally, I have adopted the third approach. I am constantly striving to maximize my life, even with the possibility of making mistakes. However, this is a decision that an adult can make. A child may not yet appreciate the consequences of the content he encounters or know how to manage it. The third approach requires honesty about failure, the ability to distinguish useful engagement from distraction, and the willingness to do Teshuvah and keep trying.

### For Children

For children, it is crucial to establish clear boundaries and introduce technology gradually, based on their maturity and responsibility levels. When my children asked for phones, I explained that when I see they are living responsible lives—abiding by their schedules, saying no to harmful behaviors, and staying motivated toward their goals—I will know they are ready to use a phone as a tool for enhancing their already structured and directed lives. Until then, it will not serve them well. They both understood this message clearly and agreed.

#### Educating Our Children About Technology

The most important aspect of educating our children about technology is honesty. This means explaining the internet and its risks openly, in a way appropriate to their age. The Torah that Hashem has given us can address the issues they face. Withholding information or pretending not to understand their questions makes it harder for them to turn to us.

We need our children to view us as relatable human beings, engaged in the struggles of life ourselves and concerned for their ultimate success. When such a relationship exists, they have someone to turn to when they encounter something confusing or inappropriate. I believe parents should begin these conversations before children are left to piece together an understanding from their peers.

### Movies, YouTube, and Video Games

#### Movies and YouTube

Media can carry ideas that conflict with Torah values even when it is not explicitly vulgar or violent. Innuendos, behavior, and the assumptions a story makes about a good life all deserve attention. When choosing something for a child to watch, look at the worldview it presents as well as its individual scenes.

#### Video Games

Video games are interactive, and some allow creativity. That alone is not a reason to treat them as beneficial or to allow unlimited use. The question is how a particular game fits into a child's life: can he stop at the agreed time, and does he still attend to his responsibilities?

Communication features matter too. Playing with others can expose a child to unfamiliar people and inappropriate language. Parents need to understand the actual game, its settings, and who their child is playing with.

#### Social Media

Social media requires particular caution. Comparison, public approval, and the pull to keep checking can become central to the experience. My approach is to keep children away from open-ended social media use. If an older child has a specific reason to use a platform, the purpose, boundaries, and adult involvement need to be clear.

#### Guidance on Media Choices

A valuable piece of advice I received from Rabbi Lippman was to review detailed descriptions of a movie's content before choosing it. Parents and children can then make an informed decision about themes such as sexual content, extreme violence, or disrespect toward others. The question is whether the particular content fits the values we are trying to live by.

### Practical Protocol

#### Create Playlists

Before letting your children watch YouTube, prepare a playlist. Choose the videos in advance so the session has a clear purpose and an endpoint. This also gives you a chance to review what they will watch.

#### Consider Peer Norms

Take into account the norms of your children's friends. A child may want to watch a show because it is part of the conversation around him. That social context deserves to be heard, even when you decide a particular show does not fit your family's boundaries.

I try to consider both the content and the child's relationship with his friends. Explain the decision honestly, and listen to what it means to him. Parents need to remain people their children can speak to about the life they are actually living.

#### Set Media Boundaries

Media consumption should be scheduled and purposeful. If a child always turns to a screen when he is bored, ask what else he wants to do with his time. In my approach, media is a privilege connected to demonstrated responsibility. It should fit into a life that already has direction.

#### Save Videos That Answer Real Questions

There is a lot of interesting content available. When children ask questions, remember to find relevant videos and save them to a playlist. That way, when they do watch something, it will address something that already interests them.

#### Keep Smartphones Out of Learning

Keep smartphones out of the learning session so the boys can attend to the learning and to one another. The current morning pods focus on Kodesh; this article describes the broader approach to technology and parenting.

A18.title: Secular Studies: Torah, Livelihood, and Real Work
A18.markdown:
## A18 Secular Studies: Torah, Livelihood, and Real Work

Route: `/blog/real-life-secular-learning-future-vision`  
Topic: Vision  
Search title: Torah, Livelihood, and Real-World Learning | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: The Academy 2027–28 vision for practical projects, entrepreneurship, financial literacy, and learning that connects responsibility with useful skills.

This article describes the [Academy 2027–28 vision](#p03-academy-202728). The current South Florida learning pods offer morning Kodesh. Practical projects and a full-day program belong to the Academy vision.

### A Father's Obligation to Teach His Son a Livelihood

Our Sages teach that a father is obligated to teach his son a trade (Kiddushin 29a). Chovot HaLevavot, Shaar HaBitachon, chapter 3, describes choosing an occupation suited to one's nature and abilities, accepting its demands, and trusting in Hashem. Livelihood can become a way to develop one's capabilities and put them to use in the world.

An education can leave a student with theoretical knowledge but little experience creating tangible value. The question we need to ask is how the skills a boy is learning will help him contribute, support himself, and take responsibility for his future family.

### Supervised Real Work Experience

In the Academy vision, students would be active contributors to meaningful work. Boys with an interest in business activities would have opportunities to learn entrepreneurship and financial literacy within a Torah-grounded environment. We believe that financial success is a tool for serving Hashem and living as a committed Jew. When a student expresses interest in building something of value, individualized guidance can help him identify personal goals, develop an idea, and refine the skills needed to bring it to life.

Responsibility has to match the individual boy's readiness. A student learning to use a tool may need close guidance. A boy who already knows how to perform a task may still need practice following through consistently. Gardening, irrigation, and drilling involve particular hard skills; independence, consistency, responsibility, and collaboration develop through repeated practice and follow-up.

### Two Forms of Practical Learning

The original vision brings together work that serves the learning community and projects that students initiate themselves.

#### Projects That Serve the Community

The Academy can become a place where boys help take care of the environment they use. Tutoring a younger student in a skill, organizing materials, maintaining a garden, or helping plan a trip gives a boy something useful to contribute. Each project needs a clear purpose, appropriate guidance, and a way to review the work.

Student budgeting, organization, decisions, and voting would take place within a defined scope. Boys need to understand what they are responsible for, what they can decide, and when an adult is responsible for the decision.

#### Independent Student Ventures

Students may also develop ideas of their own. An interest in a product, service, or small business can become a reason to learn numbers, writing, communication, planning, and the practical skills the idea requires. The educational aim is to help a boy carry an idea through into useful work, with realistic expectations and adult guidance.

### Why the Work Needs to Matter

When education feels like something being imposed on a student, he can lose sight of its value. A learning environment should help him take responsibility for what he is doing and why. The Academy vision combines student autonomy with agreed minimum commitments, so that individual direction and shared responsibility can work together.

An environment where students do real work for the benefit of the community gives them a reason to care about the outcome. With tools, materials, and coaching, they can produce something useful and see the consequences of their decisions. A garden needs tending after it has been planted. A trip plan has to fit the budget. Someone else may be relying on a task being finished.

Assignments that never connect to a purpose beyond the grade can leave students wondering why their effort matters. Practical work makes the purpose visible. It also creates a reason to return to the underlying skills: measuring accurately, writing clearly, checking a calculation, or explaining a decision.

The boys' contributions should be needed and valued. They are responsible for real tasks, given real tools, and taught how to use them. They can see the results of their contributions and experience being members of a functioning community.

### Free AI Software for Jewish Schools

The broader technology work brings the same concern for useful skills to schools and educators. Bnei Neviim offers [Free AI Software for Jewish Schools](#p10-technology): natural-language tools and custom automations intended to reduce administrative overhead.

A school can sign up and receive personal contact to discuss its needs. Understanding a real workflow, describing what needs to happen, and checking whether a tool does that job are all examples of purposeful work. These are also skills that can inform future educational projects.

The technology offer has its own page and support path. It is separate from the current morning Kodesh pods and from support for the wider Academy vision.

### Entrepreneurship and Jewish Identity

Rashi on Devarim 4:28 explains the verse's reference to serving other gods through subservience to the people who worship them. For me, this raises a broader question about livelihood: whose purposes are my time, energy, and talents advancing? That educational question is my application of the source.

Entrepreneurship gives a person an opportunity to build his own capabilities and take responsibility for the direction of his work. He has to think about the value he offers, the people he serves, and the commitments he makes. It can become an expression of his particular abilities within a life of avodas Hashem.

In our educational philosophy, secular skills are directed toward livelihood, practical responsibility, and serving Hashem. Understanding elements of the outside world can also deepen our understanding of Torah. The purpose of studying a skill should be clear to the student, and its use should remain connected to the life he is trying to build.

When students work within this framework, livelihood becomes a way to express their nikkudah—the particular contribution they can bring into the world. Guided by Torah, that work can bring their values into the physical and digital places where they earn a living.

### AI and the Future of Work

AI brings new questions into the relationship between knowledge, skill, and responsibility. As tools take on more of a task, the person using them still needs to decide what he wants to accomplish, judge the result, and take responsibility for it. The technology does not settle those questions for him.

The Academy vision emphasizes life skills, daas, and [self-governance](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education). The clarity to identify a goal, make a plan, follow through, and reconsider a mistake matters whatever tools a student uses.

The phrase I use with students is: if you can learn Gemara, you can learn anything. It is an encouragement to approach unfamiliar subjects with the same willingness to work through difficulty, ask questions, and test an explanation. Each professional field still has knowledge and skills that must be learned and practiced.

Formal qualifications should also be considered purposefully. A particular career or further study may require a credential, and some students benefit from the structure it provides. The decision should be connected to the student's goals and the actual requirements of his next step. That is part of learning to direct his own life responsibly.

## A19 Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation

Route: `/blog/ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation`

Search title: Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: Ratzon, identity, and the desire to learn: BNA's approach to connecting Torah, personal meaning, agency, and sustained responsibility.

The same behavior can come from pressure or from ratzon. A boy may sit with a sefer because he expects a prize, because he is afraid to disappoint someone, or because the question in front of him matters to him. The outward action does not reveal the whole relationship to learning.

Ratzon means will or desire. In BNA's educational approach, the question is what a boy wants to move toward and how that direction connects to Torah, his values, and his understanding of who he is.

### Interest and identification

Enjoyment of learning itself and identification with the value of learning are related, but distinct. A boy may stay with a discussion because he finds it interesting. He may also persist through a difficult passage because understanding Torah matters to the person he wants to become.

Both belong in the educational picture. Intrinsic interest gives a reason to engage with the activity itself. Identification with a purpose gives the effort a place in his life. Ratzon should not be reduced to whether he enjoys every moment.

The aim is for Torah learning and serving Hashem to become part of his own direction. A completed page matters, and so does the relationship being formed with learning.

### Torah in response to a question

A question gives learning a purpose. A disagreement, a difficulty, or an observation can lead into Torah sources that address something the boys are already trying to understand.

This is the [organic flow of Torah](#a10-torah-that-answers-real-life): following the group's questions, identifying the relevant sources, and developing the discussion. The educator brings knowledge and direction while taking the boys' actual questions seriously.

Learning can then involve curiosity, effort, disagreement, and discovery. The boy has a question to work through and a reason to pursue an answer.

### Giving ratzon practical form

Agency requires opportunities to act and commitments to follow through. Coaching connects intention with action: what was agreed, what was completed, where difficulty arose, and what comes next. Goals are considered relative to each boy's level.

A difficult beginning does not mean there is no ratzon. It may call for a clearer purpose, an attainable next step, useful support, or a conversation about what the boy actually wants.

The educator also provides a [living example](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif). Seeing someone take Torah, work, and other people seriously gives substance to the person a boy may want to become.

Ratzon gives direction to effort. The educational task is to help a boy recognize a direction he can own and develop the capacity to follow it.

Route: `/blog/responsibility-through-meaningful-contribution`  
Topic: Responsibility and Self-Governance  
Search title: Responsibility Through Meaningful Contribution | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: Responsibility develops through useful roles, clear commitments, practical contribution, and learning from the results of one's work.

Responsibility has to be practiced. Knowing what a responsible person should do is only a beginning. A boy needs a role, a purpose for that role, and an opportunity to experience what happens when he follows through or leaves the work unfinished.

BNA's approach begins with meaningful contribution. The student is needed. His work serves a real purpose within the institution, and he can see how his participation affects other people.

### A role with a purpose

A useful role makes the responsibility clear. There is something that needs to happen, someone who has agreed to take it on, and a standard by which the result can be assessed.

In the planned Academy 2027–28, this includes care of shared spaces, project organization, budgeting, trip planning, and participation in community decisions. Gardening and irrigation provide practical examples: plants need water, materials need to be organized, and a system needs to function.

The purpose of these tasks is visible. They contribute to the community's daily life. Skills are learned because the work requires them.

Agency matters here. Students participate in selecting and understanding their commitments. Once a role is accepted, its responsibilities become part of the agreement.

### Learning from the result

Real work provides feedback. An irrigation connection either supplies water where it is needed or requires adjustment. A budget either accounts for the planned expense or leaves something unresolved. A shared space is either ready for the next group or still needs attention.

The educator provides instruction, appropriate oversight, and support. The student needs room to attempt the work, make mistakes, and participate in correcting them.

Failure becomes part of the review: what happened, what was missed, what support was needed, and what needs to change. Completing the task for a boy before he can respond removes an opportunity to practice responsibility. Leaving him with a task he cannot understand removes the guidance he needs.

### Capability and follow-through

Technical ability and responsibility are assessed separately. A student may demonstrate how to use a tool correctly once. Consistent preparation, care of materials, appropriate collaboration, and independent follow-through require evidence across his work.

Review considers his level and the difficulty of the agreed task. It distinguishes what he can do from how reliably he applies that ability. A mistake informs the next step; it does not define the student.

[Self-governance](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education) develops within this relationship between agency and shared responsibility. The boy contributes to something he values, sees the effect of his choices, and has a part in improving the result.

## A22 Role Models, Or Pnimi, and Or Makif

Route: `/blog/role-models-or-pnimi-or-makif`  
Topic: Learning Environment  
Search title: Role Models, Or Pnimi, and Or Makif | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: BNA's educational use of Or Pnimi and Or Makif distinguishes instruction that becomes understood from inspiration through a living example.

An educator teaches information and skills, and also shows what a life built around Torah can look like. These are different aspects of chinuch, even when the same person provides both.

BNA uses the distinction between Or Pnimi and Or Makif to describe this relationship. This is an educational application of concepts from Chassidus: what has become understood and internalized, and what inspires a person beyond his present capacity.

### Or Pnimi: what can be internalized

Or Pnimi means internal light. In this educational application, it refers to teaching that enters the student's understanding: a word he can translate, a Rashi he can explain, a halacha he can apply, or a skill he can carry out.

Instruction has to meet the student's present level. A difficult passage may need to be divided into parts. An explanation may need an example. The educator observes what the boy can do independently and where support is still needed.

As understanding develops, the support can change. The aim is for the learning to become something the boy can use himself.

### Or Makif: what awakens aspiration

Or Makif means surrounding light. For BNA, it describes inspiration that reaches beyond what a student can yet explain or perform.

A boy may encounter someone whose seriousness in Torah, discipline in work, or conduct toward other people awakens a desire to grow. He may recognize a quality worth moving toward before he knows how to develop it.

Instruction can be broken into steps. The life being modeled remains whole. The educator can make a Rashi accessible without making his own commitment to Torah smaller. The boy can encounter that commitment and begin to imagine his own direction.

This is part of cultivating [ratzon](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation).

### The educator's example

Role modeling takes place in ordinary conduct: listening to an objection, acknowledging a mistake, caring for shared materials, keeping an agreement, and returning to a difficult question.

These moments show how the values being taught are lived. The example includes how the educator handles his own limitations and corrects his own work.

A role model does not remove the need for instruction. Inspiration needs opportunities for study, practice, and responsibility. Instruction also needs a purpose that makes the effort worth pursuing.

### Teaching at BNA

This distinction informs the educator's role at BNA: substantive Torah teaching, responsiveness to the group's questions, and individual coaching within an autonomous learning community.

When participation becomes difficult, the conversation returns to the student's commitment, the obstacle encountered, and the next practical step. Guidance should preserve dignity while taking responsibility seriously.

The educator brings both knowledge that can be understood and an example worth growing toward.

A23.title: Torah, Daas, and Inner Development
A23.markdown:
## A23 Torah, Daas, and Inner Development

Route: `/blog/torah-daas-and-inner-development`  
Topic: Torah Learning  
Search title: Torah, Daas, and Inner Development | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: BNA's Torah teaching philosophy: the relationship between spiritual influence, conscious understanding, personal questions, and Torah expressed in life.

### Two Forms of Divine Influence

Chassidus distinguishes between ממלא כל עלמין, Memaleh Kol Almin, and סובב כל עלמין, Sovev Kol Almin. Memaleh describes Divine influence received according to the capacity of each created being. Sovev describes influence that exceeds that capacity and is not consciously grasped in the same way. These are spiritual descriptions; encompassing does not mean occupying the space around an object.

The soul expresses different capacities through the eyes and the brain. This illustrates influence received according to the capacity of the recipient.

The distinction helps frame an educational question: what has a person already understood and internalized, and what is influencing or inspiring him beyond his present understanding? A person needs both. The encounter with something greater can awaken a desire to grow, while learning gives that growth a form he can understand and use.

### Mitzvos and Conscious Integration

A mitzvah has spiritual significance even when its meaning is not fully understood. At the same time, the work of avodas Hashem includes bringing more of that meaning into conscious life. A boy can learn what a mitzvah requires, consider what it expresses, and notice how it affects the way he relates to Hashem and other people.

The goal is integration: Torah knowledge becomes connected to awareness, judgment, and action. In this educational framework, daas concerns a relationship with what is known. Information has become personal enough to guide how a person lives.

This educational vision connects that process with Geulah and the coming of Moshiach: the revelation of Hashem’s oneness within the finite world. That purpose gives the work of bringing Torah and mitzvos into conscious life its wider direction.

### Torah as Guidance for the Person

The pasuk describes Torah as life and healing: כי חיים הם למצאיהם ולכל בשרו מרפא — Mishlei 4:22. The educational question is how a student encounters Torah as guidance within the life he is actually living.

A boy may understand the words of a source while remaining unsure how they relate to his own frustration, ambition, relationships, or decisions. Discussion gives those connections a place to be examined. What does the source say? What is the actual difficulty? How does the teaching change his understanding of the situation?

This is the purpose of connecting Torah study with self-awareness and practical reflection. A halacha, a passage of Mussar, or an idea in Chassidus can become relevant to a decision the boy is ready to consider. The educator helps preserve the meaning of the source while making space for that personal encounter.

### Teaching Torah as an Answer

A question gives learning direction. When a boy wants to understand a difficulty, relevant Torah sources become part of the search for an answer. The source is studied carefully, its reasoning is considered, and its implications are discussed.

That process does not depend on every boy asking the same question or reaching the same level at the same time. The educator works with the interests and understanding of the boys present. One question may open a connected subject, and the discussion can move through several sources while remaining grounded in the Torah itself.

Torah learning also carries obligations and requires sustained effort. Personal relevance gives the learner a way to participate in that effort with greater awareness. The aim is for the boy to understand more, identify with what he is learning, and increasingly direct his actions through it.

### The Educational Environment

This kind of learning requires an educator who listens, knows the sources, and lives the values being discussed. The relationship and atmosphere are part of the experience. Students need room to express a question honestly, consider an answer, and return to it as their understanding develops.

The morning Kodesh pods apply this through the [organic flow of Torah](#p02-learning-pods): questions, relevant sources, discussion, and individual guidance. The fuller [Academy 2027–28](#p03-academy-202728) vision connects that learning with practical work and responsibilities within the community.
